energy-resources-distribution-s1.title: Oil reserves, production and use in four countries

table.caption: Proven oil reserves and yearly production and use, in billions of barrels (invented data for practice)

items.q: Why are coal, oil and natural gas found in some regions and not others?
options: They form wherever the climate today is hot and dry enough for them
They are spread evenly through Earth's crust at about the same depth
They form near volcanoes, where rising magma heats buried plant material
They formed where ancient swamps or seas buried life

why.correct: Fossil fuels are the remains of organisms buried in ancient swamps and seas. They are found only where that happened and the rock layers trapped them.
options: Today's climate does not decide where ancient deposits formed.
Deposits are concentrated in basins, not spread evenly.
Volcanic heat is a separate resource (Earth's internal heat), not a source of fossil fuel deposits.
Right: geologic history decides where the deposits are.

items.q: What is a proven reserve of oil?
options: Oil stored in large tanks by a government for emergencies
Oil that has already been pumped, refined and sold to buyers
Known oil that is profitable to recover now
The total amount of oil that exists anywhere in Earth's crust

why.correct: Proven reserves are the part of a deposit that has been located and can be extracted profitably now. The number changes as prices and technology change.
options: Emergency stocks are stored oil, not reserves in the ground.
Oil already produced is no longer a reserve.
Right: known, recoverable and economic now.
Much oil is not found yet or is too costly to recover; that is not counted as proven.

items.q: Which place is best suited for large solar farms?
options: A polar region with long, dark winters and low sun angles in summer
A dry region near 25 degrees latitude with clear skies
A cloudy coastal region near 55 degrees latitude with frequent fog
A rainy tropical forest near the equator with heavy cloud cover most days

why.correct: Solar output depends on insolation. Dry subtropical regions get strong, direct sunlight and few clouds.
options: Low sun angles and long dark winters give little solar energy.
Right: high insolation and clear skies.
Clouds and lower sun angles at high latitude cut output.
Heavy cloud cover in rainforests blocks much of the sunlight.

items.q: Why do countries such as Iceland get much of their electricity and home heating from hot water and steam drawn from underground?
options: They sit on a plate boundary with hot rock near the surface
They get more sunlight than most countries, which warms the ground deeply
Their cold climate makes wells into hot rock cheaper to drill than elsewhere
Their rivers and ocean currents carry warm water up from the equator

why.correct: Iceland lies on a divergent plate boundary with volcanoes and hot spots, so very hot rock and water are close to the surface.
options: Right: plate boundaries bring Earth's internal heat near the surface.
Iceland gets little sunlight in winter; this heat comes from below.
Drilling cost depends on how deep the heat is, not on cold air.
Rivers do not carry equatorial water to Iceland.

items.q: A company wants to make electricity from a river by building a dam. Which landscape feature matters most?
options: A wide, flat plain where a slow river spreads out into channels
A dry desert basin that has no permanent rivers or streams
A flat coastal marsh near sea level with tides moving in and out
A steady river dropping steeply through a narrow valley

why.correct: The electricity depends on how much water flows and how far it falls. Steep, narrow valleys with steady flow are ideal.
options: A slow river on flat land has little drop to use.
There is no steady flow to use.
Water at sea level has almost nowhere to fall.
Right: high flow and a large drop.

items.q: A country has no fossil fuel deposits and imports all its oil. Which is a direct consequence of this uneven distribution?
options: It has no electricity until it finds oil of its own underground
Its air pollution is higher than in the countries that produce oil
Its supply and prices depend on other countries
Its people use more energy per person than people in oil-rich countries

why.correct: Importing energy ties a country to world prices, shipping and politics abroad, which is why many countries want local sources.
options: Electricity can come from many sources, including imports and renewables.
Pollution depends on how much fuel is burned, not on where it was produced.
Right: supply and price depend on other countries.
Having no fuel deposits does not raise use per person.

items.q: A country's proven oil reserves rise from 10 billion to 14 billion barrels in a year when almost no new oil is discovered. What is the most likely reason?
options: Part of the country's natural gas turned into oil during the year
Higher prices or better drilling made known oil worth recovering
New oil formed in the rock layers underground during that year
People used less oil, which added the unused oil back to the reserve

why.correct: Reserves count oil that can be recovered profitably now. A price rise or a new drilling technique moves known oil into the proven category without a new discovery.
options: Oil does not turn into gas in a year.
Right: economics and technology change what counts as proven.
Oil forms over millions of years, not in a year.
Using less oil slows the decline of reserves but does not add oil.

items.q: At its current rate of production, how many years will country X's proven oil reserves last?

mistakes.why: You multiplied. Divide the reserve by the yearly production: billion barrels over billion barrels per year leaves years.
You divided the wrong way. Put the reserve on top: reserve ÷ production per year.

items.q: Which country produces much more oil than it uses?
options: Country Y
Country Z
Country W
Country X

why.correct: Country X produces 1.2 billion barrels a year and uses 0.3, so it exports most of its oil.
options: Country Y uses 2.0 but produces 0.9, so it imports.
Country Z produces nothing and imports all it uses.
Country W produces 0.5 and uses 0.6, close to balanced.
Right: production 1.2, use 0.3.

items.q: What percent of the oil it uses does country Y import? (Imports are use minus production.)

mistakes.why: That is the percent Y produces itself. Imports are use minus production: 2.0 - 0.9.
Divide by what the country uses (2.0), not by what it produces.

items.q: Which conclusion is best supported by the table?
options: Countries with no proven reserves use no oil in a typical year
The biggest users of oil may have small reserves
Each country produces about as much oil as it uses each year
The country with the largest reserves also uses the most oil

why.correct: Country Y uses the most oil (2.0) but has far smaller reserves than X, and Z uses oil with no reserves at all.
options: Z has no reserves but uses 0.7 billion barrels a year.
Right: use and reserves are mismatched.
X and Z show large gaps between production and use.
X has the largest reserves but uses only 0.3.

items.q: According to the diagram, where are coal, oil and natural gas found?
options: In sedimentary rock layers
In the hot rock near the plate boundary
In the mud of the reservoir behind the dam
In the soil just under the open plain

why.correct: The diagram shows fossil fuels in sedimentary layers beneath the plain.
options: Right: fossil fuels lie in sedimentary basins.
Hot rock near the plate boundary is the source of Earth's internal heat.
The reservoir stores water to turn turbines at the dam.
The diagram shows the fuels deep in rock layers, not in surface soil.

items.q: Which energy resource in the diagram depends most on the region's climate rather than its rock?
options: Coal
Natural gas
Earth's internal heat
Sunlight

why.correct: The diagram links strong sunlight to dry, cloud-free, lower-latitude regions: a climate pattern.
options: Coal depends on buried ancient swamps (rock).
Natural gas depends on sedimentary basins (rock).
Earth's internal heat depends on plate boundaries (rock).
Right: solar energy depends on clouds and latitude.

items.q: A town is built on the coast shown in the diagram, far from the basin and the mountains. Which local energy source would the diagram suggest it develop first?
options: A station using heat from deep hot rock
A large dam on a steep mountain river
Wind-driven generators on the coast
A coal mine dug under the town itself

why.correct: The diagram marks coasts as windy, while coal, hot rock and steep rivers are elsewhere.
options: Hot rock is near the plate boundary in the mountains.
The steep river and dam are in the mountains.
Right: coasts have strong, steady wind.
The diagram shows the coal under the basin, not the coast.

items.q: A mountain town in the diagram wants to cut its imported diesel use. Propose a local energy source and explain why it fits this location.

why.correct: The mountains have a steep river with a dam site and hot rock near a plate boundary; either fits because the resource is right there.

source.label: Source
options: a small dam and generator on the steep river
a coal mine
an oil well

why.1: The diagram places coal in the basin far from the mountains, and coal would not cut fossil fuel use.
why.2: Oil lies in the basin, and an oil well would not reduce fossil fuel use.

why.label: Why it fits
options: water falling a long way down the valley can turn turbines all year
mountains are sunnier than any other place
fossil fuels are found under every mountain

why.1: The diagram links strong sunlight to dry low-latitude regions, not mountains.
why.2: The diagram places fossil fuels in a sedimentary basin, not under the mountains.

specific.model: The town should build a small dam and generator on the steep mountain river, because water falling a long way down the valley can turn turbines through the year, which reduces the diesel it must import.

items.q: A map shows average wind speeds: 3 m/s over a forested valley, 6 m/s over farmland and 9 m/s over an offshore shelf. Where would wind-driven generators produce the most energy?
options: The offshore shelf
The forested valley
The farmland
The three sites would produce the same

why.correct: Faster wind carries much more energy, so the 9 m/s site would produce the most.
options: Right: highest wind speed gives the most energy.
Trees slow the wind; 3 m/s is the weakest site.
Farmland is good, but 6 m/s is slower than the offshore site.
Wind speed differs, so output differs.

items.q: Why are places right at the equator often poor sites for making electricity from wind, even though they get strong sunlight?
options: Strong sunlight near the equator stops the air from moving at the surface
Wind-driven generators stop working in very hot, humid weather
The air over the tropics is held still by the Coriolis effect
Surface winds there are often weak and variable

why.correct: Rising air near the equator (the doldrums, where the Hadley cells begin) gives light, variable surface winds, though local sites can still be windy.
options: Sunlight drives wind by uneven heating; it does not stop it.
Generators work in hot climates.
The Coriolis effect turns moving air; it does not stop it, and the trade winds blow steadily across much of the tropics.
Right: equatorial surface winds are often light.
